#9419. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In a genre built around sweetness and ease, one “cozy” video game did something far greater: It put me back together after I lost Mary.

Mary was not only my then-boyfriend’s mother, but she also became an important maternal figure when my own family life felt unstable. I accompanied her on weekly grocery store runs that included stops at Marshall’s and Dollar Tree, where I’d watch her study the prices of everything from spices to bath products. When she saw me marveling at her meticulousness, she would share wise tidbits about how she looked for deals.

Our trips often ended with a late-afternoon stop at a Vietnamese restaurant, where she treated me to a warm bowl of beef pho. She’d share what she was excited to make for dinner; I was, of course, welcome to join. In these seemingly mundane afternoons, I felt cared for without the rush of obligations. Mary stopped time for me.

Last November, Mary left behind a world of loved ones after living with cancer for 14 months. From her living room to emergency stays in the hospital, I spent almost every single day of her fight by her side. Yet in my loneliest hours, I agonize over whether I fully cherished our last months together. Did I hug her enough, and did I tell her enough how much she means to me? These questions haunted me in the months afterward.

Funny enough, it wasn’t religion that rescued me; it was Pokémon Pokopia. On the surface, it is a new social simulation game featuring the iconic Japanese creatures who first took the world by storm in 1996. I first heard of its arrival on social media through gamers who raved that it was going to be the best game of the year. I grew up on Pokémon titles, so I recognized it as a distraction from my personal reckoning with abandonment.

But what began as a spur-of-the-moment decision to try what 4 million other gamers were playing turned into a transformative journey exploring what I want my life to mean when it feels as if I have been left behind.

Pokopia falls in the “cozy” game genre, beloved for its warm colors, gentle atmospheres, and easy missions. Released in March, Pokopia stars Ditto, an amorphous purple blob Pokémon that uses its transformative abilities to imitate its human trainer and rebuild a curious post-apocalyptic world devoid of human beings and Pokémon. Ditto first awakens in a cave, and as the story unfolds, the creature looks out at a once-grassy environment of parched earth and litter. It meets the first Pokémon, the hydrophilic Squirtle that teaches Ditto how to spray water across the thirsty soil to bring it back to life; it is also the only other semblance of a survivor in this barren land.

From here the story gains momentum: As Ditto, your mission is to get the environment back to habitable levels and bring back Pokémon creatures that are presumably hiding. Gradually, the unfinished railroad tracks and cracked concrete steps of a staircase stop looking like signs of a catastrophe but rather fixable problems.

I wasn’t alone in trying to find meaning after a loss or trauma. Scholars have explored a variety of constructs around the meaning of life. Psychologists Login S. George and Crystal L. Park articulate a three-part framework in their 2010 article, grounded in comprehension, purpose, and mattering, as a basis for assessing our judgments and feelings as we find meaning after loss.

At first, meaning seemed absent. I sat glued to my Nintendo Switch for three hours on my first day of play. I came up for air only when my console told me that I was low on battery. Yet I did not feel depleted; I had finished restoring the first environment in the Pokopia world to verdant levels with lush berry trees and waterfalls.

As I built new habitats, I met new Pokémon. A Charmander emerged among tall grass. A Cubone spawned from a gravesite surrounded by wildflowers. Every new Pokémon that resurfaced charmed me with their excitement to be back home, scampering across the grass to greet other familiar faces. In my mind, I thanked these creatures for turning to me. Without Ditto’s help—my help—a world of Pokemon creatures ceases to exist, fated to disappear alongside humanity.

After a Pokémon spawns in its revived habitat, it awakens with some surprise. “Huh?” “What?” Some of them startle and put up their defenses in front of Ditto, who then coaxes them into the reality that they are back in a safe, familiar home. Often this realization gives them relief. “Wow, you did all of this? Thank you!”

Some of the Pokémon seem more wistful. They hold on to items or articles of clothing that their trainer used to wear, like the oversized Tangrowth (a large Pokémon with thick, shaggy vines that cover its entire body) that wears a pair of glasses much too small for him that gamers can infer are its trainer’s. Other creatures comment on Ditto’s human-like appearance (“You look like your human!”). These private conversations between Pokémon affirm that Ditto, who is also piecing together where its own trainer has gone, is doing something meaningful.

In 2023, game scholars Karam Eum and Young Yim Doh explored how bereaved adults shaped a meaning-making experience by playing video games with narratives that focus on loss and grief. Subjects spent a week playing two different video games and kept a diary where they shared specific game scenes that were particularly meaningful. While the games did evoke sad memories, participants also recalled positive memories in their pre- and post-loss lives, be it a funny conversation or a serendipitous moment shared with close ones who are still alive.

In the real world, the player behind the console, I, too, wonder where my beloved human has gone. I see Mary in the pink rose bouquets at grocery stores, and I smell her in the fragrant bone broth that wafts from the next-door apartment unit. In some of these most visceral disruptions, I feel my loss painfully.

But even in these heaviest of days, I surrender to the ordinary surprises that come up: a call from an old neighbor asking if I can help make meals for a family in need, or a stray cat mewing at my window to open the building’s front gate. I am startled out of a detached state, and I am moved to help, the way I got to help Mary.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

I associate Mary now with the colorful berry trees in Pokopia. When I come across one that needs tending, I remember how easy it is to water it with my Squirtle-like powers. When I clear a path from blocks of beach sand to make way for a new house for my aquatic Pokémon, I think of Mary’s selfless endeavors to nourish and comfort all of her friends and family.

Despite its sad undertones, Pokopia is full of positive quests, eager to help gamers imbue its universe with the belief that it is worth building a positive world in memory of those who shaped us. Even though our loved ones may “mysteriously” leave us behind, we recreate happiness, redefine ourselves, and choose who and what we live for, even if they do not come back.

It’s curious to me that bereavement can feel so isolating, although it is a human experience universally experienced. It helps to have a video game that reminds me of the actual truth. When I start to catch myself drifting into deeper ends of grief, I have something to divert my attention: I wonder how my Ditto is doing? I pick up my Switch 2 that sits at the foot of my bed, and I make a new home for my Pokémon the way Mary had done for me.

Lisa Kwon is an arts and culture writer based in Los Angeles, CA. She has contributed to The Guardian, Teen Vogue, Vulture, Eater, Prism Reports, Cultured Magazine, National Geographic, and many more.

When we go straight to analyzing our own grief or someone else's, we are skipping an important step.

#9418. Your brain may not actually “make” decisions

What we experience when making a decision may be very different from what actually happens inside the brain, according to Indiana University Professor Tom James.

For decades, both scientific theories and everyday intuition have tended to describe decision-making as a sequence. First we perceive something, then we think about it and make a choice, and finally we act. Each step is often assumed to correspond to a distinct brain function, moving from sensory processing to cognition and then to motor activity.

Many scientific approaches, particularly model-based cognitive neuroscience, are built around this same linear framework. It also matches how decision making feels from the inside. As James notes, "Our actions feel like they are caused by decisions based on desires, beliefs, and intentions."

Rethinking the Brain's Decision Making Process

James argues that this familiar explanation, sometimes called the "sandwich model," does not fit neatly with what scientists know about the brain. Sensation has identifiable sensory mechanisms, and action has identifiable motor mechanisms. But the supposed cognitive stage between the two does not appear to have a corresponding neural process that functions as a distinct decision maker.

Rather than proposing a dedicated decision-making system that directs behavior, James suggests that sensory, sensorimotor, and motor processes together produce what he calls 'action selection.' In this view, behavior emerges through ongoing interactions among the brain, body, and environment. These processes can occur simultaneously and feed back into one another rather than unfolding as a simple sequence.

That does not mean James believes decisions are unreal.

As James says, "Of course they do. We use this language all the time and it's very helpful in terms of describing behavior. The leap, I think, is to say that the brain works by having decision-making or control processes. It produces behavior that is well described in that way. But it doesn't need a process that does that to make it look that way."

James, a professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences in the College of Arts and Sciences, presents the argument in "Sensorimotor Mechanisms of Decisions and Actions," an article just published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience.

What Happens in the Brain When We Make a Decision?

James develops his argument using a "physicalist" framework associated with philosophers such as Daniel Dennett. The approach makes explicit what James sees as a basic assumption underlying science: physical phenomena can cause both physical and nonphysical phenomena, while nonphysical phenomena cannot themselves cause physical events.

Sensory and motor processes, for example, are physical. Decisions, in this framework, are nonphysical. If that is the case, James argues, a decision cannot literally cause a physical action.

To make the idea easier to understand, he uses several analogies.

Drawing on Daniel Dennett's comparison between the self and a center of mass (CoM) or center of gravity, James suggests that decisions may function in a similar way. A center of mass is a useful mathematical concept, but it cannot independently exert a physical force. (i.e., you cannot move an object's center of mass without moving the object) In the same sense, James proposes that a decision may be an abstract description rather than a physical entity that directly causes something to happen.

Another analogy shows how useful concepts can become less informative when scientists need to understand events at a more detailed level.

We routinely use the phrase "the university" to describe the activities of an institution. The term conveniently represents a collection of people, buildings, departments, and processes. Saying that "the university took certain actions during a campus protest," however, tells us little about the specific events involved. A detailed explanation might instead require examining meetings between administrators, phone calls to state police, and other individual actions.

James argues that decisions present a similar problem for neuroscience. They may provide a useful high-level description of behavior without revealing the physical mechanisms producing it.

As James maintains: "As mental phenomena, they are defined on too abstract a level for the goals of cognitive neuroscience."

In other words, simply saying that someone made a decision does not explain what happened inside the brain.

James uses a third example to push the argument further.

He points to a robot constructed from a small number of sensory, motor, and sensorimotor modules. The machine demonstrates "wall-following" behavior that can appear purposeful. From the outside, it seems to have goals, strategies, and perhaps even something resembling intentions.

But the robot contains no system designed to make decisions.

"The robot does not have decisions built into it," James explains. "It just senses its environment and moves around accordingly. And based on the environment, wall-following turns out to be a good thing. It looks intentional. It looks strategic. It looks like the robot is making decisions. And yet, it is not. The reason we know it is not is that there are no systems built into it to do that."

That raises a provocative question. If a relatively simple machine can produce behavior that looks intentional without possessing a decision-making system, could human behavior also appear to result from centralized decisions even if no such central process exists?

James argues that this explanation is more parsimonious than assuming the brain contains what he calls "a higher-level, central controller that monitors and regulates sensory and motor processes."

The idea of a central controller also creates a philosophical problem that has been discussed since the time of Descartes.

If some higher-level entity inside the brain is responsible for observing information and deciding what to do, scientists still need to explain how that controller itself works.

"Explaining that the brain works by way of a central controller suggests that you haven't figured out how the brain works, because you've just put a person inside your brain," says James. "Dennett called this idea the Cartesian Theater. That person inside your brain would need another person inside its brain, which would need a person inside its brain and so on, in an infinite regress. So the problem is never solved. It's just passed on."

Instead of invoking an internal decision maker, James proposes focusing directly on the interacting sensory and motor systems that generate behavior.

If decision making emerges from continuous interactions among the brain, body, and environment, studying it will require experimental methods capable of capturing that complexity.

James acknowledges that this creates both exciting opportunities and difficult methodological challenges. Researchers would need to move beyond strictly linear models and examine processes that happen simultaneously, influence one another, and change as a person interacts with the surrounding world.

His own laboratory has begun exploring this direction by drawing on ideas from embodied cognition and ecological psychology.

James believes this approach could help cognitive neuroscience uncover the mechanisms that give rise to what we describe as decision-making. It may also offer new ways to investigate many other cognitive and mental phenomena that have traditionally been treated as distinct processes inside the brain.

Materials provided by Indiana University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9416. What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.

A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”

I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.

I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim, or contact campus or local police departments.

This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?

Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.

Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.

The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.

Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence—even when this belief is wrong—inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.

Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed—in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.

Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.

This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.

Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program—focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors—report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later.

These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior.

At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.

But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team.”

Another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. Bystander intervention programs emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence.

Students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.

It’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only with college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up.

Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling—and learning specific strategies for intervening—can make a real difference.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

is the Poler Family Professor of Psychology at Amherst College. Her latest trade book, published in North America as Why We Act: Turning Bystanders Into Moral Rebels (Harvard University Press) and internationally as The Bystander Effect: The Psychology of Courage and Inaction (HarperCollins), examines why good people so often stay silent or do nothing in the face of wrongdoing.

#9415. Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells

Severe stress during childhood can increase a person's vulnerability to anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders when new challenges arise later in life. Scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and Princeton University have now identified a biological process that may help explain how early trauma can have such long-lasting effects on the brain.

Researchers have known that stress during early development can alter gene activity in the brain. The new findings suggest that these changes stem partly from the way brain cells package their DNA. By making certain stress-related genes easier to activate, early adversity may leave the brain more reactive and less able to tolerate future stress.

The study was published Aug. 7 in Neuron.

"We have uncovered a new biological process linking experience of early-life adversity to this long-term vulnerability to mental illness," said Meaghan Creed, PhD, an associate professor of anesthesiology at WashU Medicine and the study's co-corresponding author. "This finding reveals a physical scar left by trauma experienced during development inside brain cells, providing scientists with a concrete biological target to develop new treatments and interventions."

How Childhood Stress Changes DNA Packaging

More than half of children worldwide experience some form of early-life stress, including abuse, violence, or drug use within the household, and other traumatic events. Experiencing four or more of these adverse events is associated with a sharply higher risk of physical and mental health problems later in life.

To understand how these experiences can physically alter the developing brain, the researchers focused on the ventral tegmental area. This brain region contains neurons that produce dopamine, a chemical messenger involved in processing important experiences, including rewards and adversity. When stress causes these neurons to become abnormally active, reward processing can be disrupted, potentially increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression.

The team then examined the epigenome inside these dopamine-producing neurons. The epigenome consists of molecular tags that help control whether genes are switched on or off, ultimately influencing how cells behave.

Catherine Jensen Peña, PhD, an assistant professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute and the study's senior and co-corresponding author, compared DNA inside cells to a coiled slinky. DNA is wrapped around proteins called histones, which help control how tightly or loosely it is packed. When this genetic slinky is tightly compressed, genes are less accessible and remain switched off. When the structure loosens and opens, the genes become easier for the cell to activate.

SETD7 Primes Brain Cells for Future Stress

In young mice exposed to stress, the researchers found elevated levels of an enzyme called SETD7 in dopamine neurons compared with mice raised under typical conditions. SETD7 helps add a chemical marker called H3K4me1 to the DNA packaging system. According to Peña, this tag encourages the genetic structure to open, making the cell more responsive to what is happening in its environment.

To test whether SETD7 itself could produce these changes, the scientists artificially increased the enzyme in young mice that had not experienced early-life stress. As the animals matured, their dopamine-producing brain cells developed a more open DNA structure, making stress response genes easier to activate.

These mice also became less tolerant of stress as adults. Animals that had elevated SETD7 levels when they were young developed more reactive dopamine neurons and showed more anxious behavior than mice whose SETD7 levels remained normal throughout life.

The researchers then tested the opposite approach. After early-life stress, they prevented SETD7 from adding excessive amounts of the H3K4me1 marker. This kept the DNA structure more tightly closed and protected the mice from becoming unusually sensitive to stress later in life.

Even after experiencing stress both early in development and again as adults, mice with reduced SETD7 activity behaved much like unstressed animals. They remained similarly social and exploratory, while activity in their dopamine neurons stayed at normal levels.

The results suggest that SETD7 and the changes it produces in DNA packaging may help create a lasting molecular memory of early adversity. They also give researchers a specific biological pathway to investigate as a possible target for future interventions.

"There are currently no treatments for what early-life stress does to the brain, partially because we have not had a clear picture of what molecular mechanisms to target," Peña said. "This work is exciting because it reveals a clear mechanism, and also helps explain why the impact of stress is both latent and broad. Additionally, if we can step in with supportive care, therapy or social resources to buffer children during those sensitive windows of development, we may be able to protect the epigenome -- preventing the genetic slinky from locking into an open position and perhaps giving the developing brain a chance to build natural resilience."

Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9414. ADHD and the Social Processing Gap

“There’s a difference between having social skills and being able to use them consistently in the moment. This is the fundamental challenge for people living with ADHD.”

“Knowing social expectations versus implementing them in real time is a very big challenge for people with ADHD.” — Sharon Saline, Psy.D.

This tension is at the heart of many slip-ups — from oversharing and interrupting to difficulties reading the room — that stump adults with ADHD across various scenarios. Dr. Saline, a clinical psychologist who specializes in ADHD, described this as the “social processing gap” during her October ADDitude webinar, “Reading Body Language & Social Cues: A Primer for People with ADHD.”

Here, learn more about the gap and how to fill it, along with quick tips for navigating sticky social situations with ease and confidence.

ADHD symptoms and traits — like working memory challenges, distractibility, impulsivity, hyperfocus and more — directly impact communication and social skills. But there’s another factor that tends to influence social interactions: shame.

We asked: Which of the following social challenges prompted you to be here today — for yourself or someone important to you? (Select all that apply.)

A history of negative and uncomfortable social interactions means that many adults with ADHD approach social situations assuming they’ll misread a facial expression, take up too much of the conversation, or commit a faux pas. As a result, many are unable to fully participate in conversations without extreme vigilance and/or becoming overwhelmed, anxious, self-conscious, or exhausted.

“ADHD affects our ability to interpret social information when it’s occurring in real time, because of anxiety and rejection sensitivity that complicate those interpretations and how people respond,” Saline said.

Navigating misunderstandings in relationships, friendships, family, and work comes down to three words: Notice. Check. Clarify.

Noticing, or building social awareness, doesn’t mean scanning for signs of disapproval. It is being attuned to other people and adapting to connection, without taking things too personally or making assumptions. “The challenge is to notice these cues without automatically assuming that they’re bored, annoyed, or rejecting us,” Saline said.

That’s where clarification comes in. Uncertainty is a potent trigger for rejection sensitivity, so Saline encourages respectful questioning to address assumptions. For example, if your partner says they’re not upset but their tone sounds irritated, ask, “I’m hearing something different in your tone. Is there something you’d like to talk about?”

#9413. Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster

A new analysis of biological aging across the human body suggests that both sleeping too little and sleeping too much are associated with faster aging in the brain, heart, lungs, immune system, and other organs. These sleep patterns were also linked to a broad range of diseases.

"Previous studies have found that sleep is largely linked to aging and the pathological burden of the brain. Our study goes further and shows that too little and too much sleep are associated with faster aging in nearly every organ, supporting the idea that sleep is important in maintaining organ health within a coordinated brain-body network, including metabolic balance and a healthy immune system," says study leader Junhao Wen, assistant professor of radiology at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

Scientists are increasingly using aging clocks to estimate whether a person is aging biologically faster or slower than their chronological age. These tools rely on machine learning and biological information (e.g., proteins from a minimally invasive blood test) to calculate patterns associated with aging.

Many aging clocks provide a single measure for the entire body. However, different organs can age at different speeds. One familiar example is the decline in ovarian function that contributes to the biological clock associated with female fertility.

Wen and his colleagues have been developing aging clocks that focus on individual organs. The goal is to provide more detailed and potentially more personalized information about a person's health.

"Everyone is excited by these aging clocks and their ability to predict disease and mortality risk," Wen says. "But to me, the more exciting question is, can we link aging clocks to a lifestyle factor that can be modified in time to slow aging?"

Sleep offered researchers an ideal way to explore that question because mounting evidence suggests that sleep plays an important role in health. Wen also had a personal interest in the issue.

"I'm also a light sleeper and was getting worried about the effects on myself," says Wen.

To create the aging clocks, Wen used information from about half a million participants in the UK Biobank. Machine learning was applied to identify biological signatures associated with aging in different organs.

The researchers built clocks using several types of information, including structural measurements from medical imaging, proteins associated with specific organs, and molecules detected in the blood.

"In the liver, for example, we have an aging clock built with protein data, an aging clock of metabolic data, and an aging clock of imaging data," Wen says. "This allows us to see whether sleep is distinctively associated with aging clocks derived from multiple omics and molecular layers."

The team then compared sleep duration (as reported by each Biobank participant) with biological age estimates from 23 aging clocks covering 17 organ systems.

Too Little and Too Much Sleep Linked to Faster Aging

A clear U-shaped pattern appeared across the body. People reporting short sleep (fewer than 6 hours) and long sleep (greater than 8 hours) tended to show faster biological aging.

The lowest levels of aging were seen among people who reported sleeping between 6.4 and 7.8 hours each day.

Importantly, the findings do not show that sleep duration by itself causes organs to age faster or slower. Instead, they suggest that sleeping either too little or too much could be a sign of poorer health throughout the body.

Sleep Duration Tied to Diseases Across the Body

The results also point to a broad connection between sleep, the brain, and the rest of the body.

Short sleep was significantly associated with depressive episodes and anxiety disorders, consistent with earlier research connecting insufficient sleep with mental health problems.

It was also associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and heart arrhythmias.

Both short and long sleep were linked to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma. They were also associated with several digestive disorders, including gastritis and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Wen says, "The broad brain-body pattern is important because it tells us that sleep duration is a deeply embedded part of our entire physiology, with far-reaching implications across the body."

The organ-specific aging clocks may also help scientists understand how sleep is connected to individual diseases. Wen and his colleagues explored this possibility by examining late life depression.

The researchers could not establish whether differences in sleep duration caused late life depression or whether depression itself changed how long people slept.

To investigate further, the team used "mediation analysis" to examine whether biological aging might help explain the relationship between short or long sleep and late life depression.

The results suggested that short sleep may be more directly connected with the burden of late-life depression. Long sleep, in contrast, may influence depression through pathways reflected in aging clocks for the brain and adipose tissue.

"This has a strong implication for future sleep management and future therapeutics," Wen says. "Our study suggests there may be different biological pathways between long and short sleepers that lead to the same outcome, late-life depression, and we shouldn't treat them the same way."

#9412. New Research Strengthens the Case for Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD Criteria

The new “severe-combined” ADHD subtype identified in a landmark study is marked by emotional dysregulation, a symptom the DSM-5 doesn’t include in its diagnostic criteria.

When the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) was updated in 2022, officials believed that research was lacking to expand ADHD’s definition to include the common and extremely impairing symptom of emotional dysregulation. Consequently, the overwhelming and uncontrollable emotions reported by many patients remain largely unrecognized as ADHD manifestations.

Now research appears to be catching up to patient reports.

A new landmark study has revealed three ADHD subtypes that reflect neurobiological differences: predominantly inattentive; predominantly hyperactive/impulsive; and the new severe-combined, which is marked by emotional dysregulation.1

Using neuroimaging and computational modeling to map the pathways of ADHD, researchers found that the severe-combined type had 45 areas of brain abnormality tied to emotion and control compared with 26 each for the two other types. The study, which analyzed 1,154 brain scans of children and adolescents with ADHD, was published recently in JAMA Psychiatry.

The findings are “an example of recent insights emerging from neuroimaging that may impact clinical care, which has been an elusive goal,” says F. Xavier Castellanos, M.D., professor emeritus of child and adolescent psychiatry at New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine. He was part of the working group that contributed to the DSM-5.

[Get This Free Download: Emotional Regulation & Anger Management Scripts]

“Still, it’s too early to assume that their intriguing results are real in the sense of replicating repeatedly in independent datasets, particularly by investigators who are not allied or collaborating with the original research team,” says Castellanos. He, like the study authors, calls for prospective studies to validate their biotypes and determine whether they may influence treatment.

Findings that reveal a new severe-combined subtype may come as no surprise to the thousands of parents of children with ADHD, and adults with the condition, who have named emotional dysregulation as the most impairing feature of ADHD in ADDitude surveys.

But, as David Anderson, Ph.D., senior psychologist at the ADHD and Behavior Disorders Center at the Child Mind Institute, points out, parents’ anecdotal feedback precedes scientific validation.

“Finding evidence of a subtype in the brain leaves open questions about the balance of nature versus nurture. Is there a biological basis for subtypes and is it reliable across the span of development?” Anderson asks. “Emotion dysregulation can be biological for kids who are more prone to emotional behavior from an early age, while some are frustrated with the world due to negative feedback they’ve gotten since kindergarten, so it’s environmental. There are multiple pathways to come to this.”

[Read: The Key to ADHD Emotional Regulation? Cultivating Gratitude, Pride & Compassion]

If the study’s findings are replicated, Castellanos says, it would become a new presentation in a future version of the DSM. “I served on the DSM-5 committee, and we were explicitly reminded that the DSM follows the field; it does not lead it. It’s only when the scientific evidence is strongly supportive that DSM changes are allowed. Otherwise, it’s too disruptive.”

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., distinguished professor at SUNY Upstate Medical University, said he believes that emotional dysregulation was not included in the DSM-5 because it might have made differential diagnosis with anxiety and mood disorders more difficult, especially in primary care. He also said he was skeptical that ADHD can be divided into biological subtypes, adding that underlying ADHD brain mechanisms exist along a spectrum and do not fall neatly into separate categories.

The study’s researchers said the findings may eventually create a path toward developing personalized therapeutic strategies.

Carole Fleck is Editor-in-Chief at ADDitude magazine.

#9411. For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

In this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

After those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually showed greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, showed no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”

There’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups showed improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

The takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

In the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them new to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.)

What did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators showed greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

But that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups showed similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

So if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

If you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out.   Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

After two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another showed that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

Why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

The benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

Imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were new to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

For beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

But do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

The idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, big-picture insights.

When researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits.   So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

A study of 38,000 people around the world finds that people who feel connected to nature are more hopeful, purposeful and resilient.

Whether we’ve been trying to improve our exercise, eating, sleep, or happiness, self-reflection is one of the most practical tools we have.

#9410. 5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is important for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9409. When Your Loved Ones Are Your Child’s Biggest Critic

ADDitude readers share the hurtful ways family and friends treat their neurodivergent children, from spewing ignorant comments to purposefully excluding them, and how they combat them.

ADHD understanding has improved in recent decades, but many people still just don’t get it – and sometimes those people are the ones closest to us.

Hearing your child criticized or misjudged hurts. Hearing criticisms and barbs from family members and friends who don’t understand ADHD ushers in a complicated whirlwind of emotions. You may feel like an inadequate parent. You may worry whether your child will be accepted at family get-togethers. You may grow weary of explaining your child’s condition.

If this is you, you’re not alone. More than 73% of ADDitude readers say they have relatives or friends who criticize or dislike their neurodivergent child. Read about their experiences and how they navigate them below.

“The older generations are close-minded or under-educated about ADHD and make it seem like it’s made up or an excuse. They say, ‘Everyone says they have ADHD’ or ‘You need to be a better parent.’ I am mostly there to protect my children and correct the person who says it, so my kids don’t feel they are less than.” – Gina, California

“I had a friend who would sugar up my kids intentionally to ‘prove’ that I was over-reacting about the negative side effects of sugar. When the kids misbehaved, she blamed it on my ‘inconsistent parenting’ and not the ADHD brain on sugar and food-coloring!” – An ADDitude Reader

[Get This Free Download: 13 Parenting Strategies for Kids with ADHD]

“We’ve had to deal with side remarks at times from relatives and friends. One example would be someone making retorts to their child like ‘Hey, what are you doing? Even John Doe (my son) would behave better than you right now.’ It’s using my son’s negative behaviors as a frame of reference that my wife and I don’t find helpful at all.” – Jono, Canada

“When my daughter was younger, I was still learning how to handle her behavior, but having family and others say that she was out of control, and that I let her get away with behaviors, really hurt. It made me feel like a bad parent. It took years of working with therapists for me to understand that her behavior and diagnosis were not my fault.” – Deneise, West Virginia

“They just don’t seem to understand that ADHD behaviors aren’t always choices. The only solution seems to be limiting time with the people who don’t understand. Plus, now that the kids are older. I explain to them that some people don’t understand.” – Jenny, Virginia

“My sister-in-law criticizes the amount of ‘stuff’ my children have and their ongoing projects. She doesn’t understand that ADHD brains organize differently and create on a whim, or that having the freedom to be creative is where they excel. I usually head off these comments by talking up their creativity and explaining that they are just brilliantly wired differently.” – An ADDitude Reader, Kansas

“My grandparents and siblings definitely thought we were failing at parenting for a while, and a few friends thought I was a bad mom. Most comments centered on not having strict enough rules/seeing my children’s behavior as bad or rude choices vs. dysregulated behaviors. My village now is almost entirely made up of parents of neurodivergent kids, and we’re all so supportive and understanding of how hard everyone works to provide support and education for our children.” – Acadia, Virginia

“My parents say my child is just lazy in school, and he needs to put more effort into everything. So sometimes I just stop telling them the details. For example, in addition to ADHD, my son recently got diagnosed with dyslexia. I won’t tell them. It’s unfortunate, because he is their grandson and they should know, but I just don’t want to discuss it anymore.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I remind them that they have never parented a child with ADHD, so they do not know what it is like to walk in my shoes. I have also sent them articles about ADHD.” – Sarah, Indiana

“Our dearest friends of 20+ years stopped inviting us to their home for Thanksgiving after a particularly difficult time in their home with our children… The best I have been able to engage with them about this is to ask how their nephew who lives in a different city and is also neurodivergent is doing. When they share difficult times in his regard, I focus the discussion on the antecedents to the disruptive behaviors and try to engage them in problem-solving sleuthing. I connect the conversation with my own experience and invite them to do the same. I have had some deep and meaningful conversations with them over the years, but we still are no longer invited to their home.” – Robyn, North Carolina

“I eventually just cut my family off from contact. The pain they caused my kids was not worth maintaining those relationships.” – Christina, Arizona

#9408. Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth

Many important choices seem to pit reason against emotion. Popular culture often describes that tension as a contest between two parts of the brain: a newer, more advanced center for rational thought and an ancient "lizard brain" that runs on instinct.

But the evolutionary history of the brain appears to be far more complicated than a simple struggle between old and new.

"There was a theory proposed in the '50s that the brain evolved in layers starting with basic bodily functions, to emotions in the reptilian brain, leading up to sophisticated reasoning in humans," explains Nabil Imam, an assistant professor in the School of Computational Science and Engineering and a faculty member with Georgia Tech's Institute for Neuroscience, Neurotechnology, and Society (INNS). "This is not how an evolutionary biologist would think about the problem."

Research published in Science Advances suggests that brain evolution may be better understood in terms of wiring rather than newer regions being stacked on top of older ones.

By examining the organization of both biological brains and artificial neural networks, Imam and his colleagues found evidence that evolution may involve allocating a limited amount of brain space among competing wiring strategies. Their model describes a computational tug of war between two fundamentally different kinds of neural organization, both of which are established even before birth.

The findings could help explain a long-running puzzle in brain evolution and may also point toward new ways of building AI systems that use less data and energy.

Terms such as "logical brain" and "lizard brain" actually refer to groups of brain regions with very different functions. The neocortex, often associated with higher-level thought, forms the outer layer of the brain and is involved in vision, perception, reasoning, and other complex abilities.

The so-called lizard brain is harder to define so neatly.

"The limbic system, sometimes called the 'reptilian brain,' controls emotion broadly speaking -- but it also has other components with distinct functions," explains Imam. The system contains separate regions involved in memory, smell, navigation, and emotional regulation. "Why do people group all these different regions into one big system? There hasn't been a good theory for what is common between these different circuits."

To explore that question, the researchers compared how these brain systems change across species. Rather than looking at individual regions one at a time, they examined how the limbic system and neocortex vary together over evolutionary history.

A clear pattern emerged. When one part of the limbic system was relatively large, the other limbic regions also tended to be larger. At the same time, the neocortex was generally smaller.

That suggests the regions are not evolving independently.

"Rather," says Imam, "it's a coordinated expansion of these regions across species."

The pattern points to the limbic system behaving more like an integrated network than a collection of unrelated structures. Across evolution, its different components appear to expand and contract together.

The next question was what might cause that coordinated shift.

Imam's explanation centers on the way different brain systems are wired before birth.

Neural circuits in the neocortex are arranged as spatial maps. Brain regions that process nearby parts of the body, such as the thumb and index finger, are also located near one another. Similar spatial organization appears in systems that handle sight and sound.

The limbic system is organized differently. Instead of being laid out spatially, its wiring works more like a bar code, with distributed patterns of activity representing particular smells or complex memories.

The researchers used AI models to test whether these differences arise from built-in architecture or are mainly learned through experience.

When an AI network was created with localized, spatial connections, it was naturally well suited to processing vision, sound, and touch. In contrast, distributed "barcode-style" networks were necessary for strong performance on smell recognition and memory.

An Evolutionary Competition for Brain Space

The researchers then investigated why the relative size of these brain systems changes so consistently among species.

The basic idea is that the brain has limited resources. Space and energy are finite, so natural selection may favor whichever wiring system is most useful for survival in a particular environment.

To test this, the team created a multimodal artificial network in which spatial and distributed systems competed for "real estate."

When the simulated environment rewarded smell, every region within the distributed system expanded while the neocortex became smaller. When vision was favored instead, the pattern reversed.

This trade-off may help explain striking differences between real animals. The nine-banded armadillo, which depends heavily on smell, has a very large limbic system. The squirrel monkey, which relies strongly on vision, has a brain dominated by the neocortex.

Across the 182 species included in the study, the findings suggest that brain evolution is less about adding progressively newer layers of "logic" and more about shifting space between different wiring systems according to what helps an animal survive.

The same principle may have implications beyond biology.

If engineers can reproduce some of this built-in neural organization in artificial intelligence, they may be able to create systems that learn more like biological brains and require far less training data and energy.

"Today's artificial neural networks are trained by vast amounts [of] data -- it's about nurture," says Imam. "But the brain is not a blank slate that gets trained by experience. It is a mix of nature and nurture, and the nature is that pre-wired architecture."

"We could translate that architecture to AI systems to make it more brain-like, or make it learn or function as efficiently as the brain."

This work was a collaboration with Cornell University and was supported by the National Science Foundation.

#9407. What is a circadian rhythm disorder? Plus, 6 ways to treat it

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You’re tired when you should be awake, or wired when you should be asleep. Whether it’s 2am and you’re staring at the ceiling, your body still hasn’t recovered from that red-eye flight, or the night shift is taking its toll, the struggle is the same: your internal clock and your life are pulling in opposite directions.

These are circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs), and they happen when your body's sleep-wake cycle doesn't match your daily schedule. And they're more common than you'd think — often mistaken for stress or brushed off as one more thing to deal with once life slows down.

The good news is that CRSDs are medically recognized and treatable. Below, we’ll cover the different types, why they happen, and how to get your sleep back on track.

Your body has an internal clock—the circadian rhythm—that regulates when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. It runs on roughly a 24-hour cycle, shaped by external cues like light, temperature, and meal timing.

A circadian rhythm sleep disorder (CRSD) occurs when your internal clock consistently falls out of sync with your environment, social schedule, or desired sleep times.

There are several distinct types of circadian rhythm sleep disorders:

Delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD): Sleep comes much later than usual (often in the early hours of the morning) followed by a struggle to wake up on time.

Advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD): Sleep arrives early in the evening, and waking happens in the early hours of the morning — the reverse of DSPD.

Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder: Sleep and wake times drift later or earlier each day instead of settling into a 24-hour rhythm. This pattern is most common in people who are blind.

Irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder: Sleep is broken into several short stretches across the day and night, without a clear pattern.

Shift work disorder: Night or rotating shift schedules conflict with the body's natural sleep timing.

Jet lag disorder: A temporary misalignment between the body’s internal clock and local time after crossing time zones.

Symptoms vary based on the type of CRSD, but the core issue is the same: sleep happens at the wrong time.

trouble falling asleep at a normal bedtime

difficulty waking up in the morning, or waking too early

mood changes, including irritability, anxiety, or low mood

Circadian rhythm sleep disorders often stem from multiple factors at once, ranging from lifestyle and environment to biology.

Light exposure: Light entering your eyes is the strongest external cue for your internal clock to stay in sync with the outside world. Too much bright light at night, like from screens, or too little natural light in the morning can push your clock in the wrong direction.

Genetics: Your genes can set your natural sleep timing earlier or later than average. Certain gene variants have been linked to differences in circadian timing, which may explain a lifelong tendency toward being a night owl or an early riser.

Age: Your sleep timing usually changes with age. Teenagers drift toward later sleep and wake times, while older adults often feel tired earlier in the evening and wake earlier as a result.

Shift work and irregular schedules: Night or rotating shifts keep you awake when your body expects to be asleep. Irregular eating and exercise can add to that disruption.

Neurological conditions: Conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or a history of traumatic brain injury are tied to a higher risk of circadian disruption, including fragmented or irregular sleep. Researchers are still working out whether disrupted rhythms are a cause, an early sign, or both.

Blindness: Without light entering the eyes, the brain's clock loses its main external cue for staying aligned with a 24-hour day.

No matter which type of CRSD you're dealing with, you can get your internal clock back on track. Here's what works, and how to find the right approach for you.

In the morning: Bright daylight early in the day helps advance your clock, which is especially useful for delayed sleep phase disorder. During darker months, using a bright light therapy box (10,000 lux) for 20–30 minutes after waking can substitute for sunlight. If you have any eye conditions, it's a good idea to check with a doctor before starting.

In the evening: Reduce bright light 2–3 hours before bed to ease your body into sleep mode. Screens and overhead lighting can suppress melatonin production, while dimmer, warmer light helps your body settle down.

Traveling across time zones? The strategy for beating jet lag with light depends on which direction you're flying. Seek bright light in the new morning and avoid it in the new evening when flying east. Do the reverse when flying west. A day or two of light timing can speed up your adjustment.

💙 Pair your morning light with a Morning Meditation from the Daily Calm.

One of the most effective ways to steady your circadian rhythm is to maintain a regular sleep schedule. Wake up at the same time every day—even on weekends—to give your body a consistent cue to work with. It may feel hard at first, but with consistency, your body naturally adjusts to the rhythm.

Working nights or rotating shifts? "Consistent" doesn't have to mean conventional. Try anchoring your sleep to the same block of hours on workdays, and limiting how far you drift on days off.

💙 Build a sleep routine with Making Progress from the 7 Days of Sleep series on Calm.

Chronotherapy involves slowly adjusting your sleep and wake times in one direction, a little each day, until you reach your target schedule.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? This might mean going to bed a few hours later each day (moving all the way around the clock) until you land on your desired bedtime. It's a demanding process, and there's some risk of your schedule drifting further off track, so it's best done under a sleep specialist's guidance rather than on your own.

A sleep specialist can help tailor chronotherapy to your specific pattern.

Sleep difficulties often come with anxiety about sleep itself, which can make it harder to fall asleep. Mindfulness practices can help calm your racing mind and relieve that anxiety. Even a few minutes of mindful breathing or a short guided meditation can quiet your mind enough to help you drift off.

💙 Try this Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

Melatonin is a hormone your brain produces, and its levels naturally rise in the evening — signaling to your body that sleep time is approaching. Think of a melatonin supplement as a timing tool rather than a sedative that will help you fall asleep on the spot.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? Take a low dose (around 0.5–3 mg) three hours before your desired bedtime to help adjust your clock gradually. A doctor or sleep specialist can advise on the right amount for your situation.

Traveling across time zones? Melatonin taken around your target bedtime (about an hour before) in the new time zone is a well-supported way to adjust to jet lag faster.

💙 Discover the best time to take melatonin for restful sleep.

For persistent or severe circadian rhythm sleep disorders, professional support can make a real difference. A sleep specialist may recommend a formal evaluation, actigraphy (a wrist sensor that tracks sleep-wake patterns over time), or a combination of treatments.

Struggling with non-24-hour or irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder? These patterns respond less predictably to light and schedule changes on their own. A sleep specialist can build a plan around your specific pattern.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is also sometimes paired with circadian-focused treatments. It’s a structured therapy that targets the thoughts and habits keeping you awake.

Several everyday habits can throw off your circadian rhythm, including irregular sleep schedules, shift work, jet lag, too much screen use at night, and inconsistent light exposure. Stress, alcohol, caffeine, and some medications can also throw off your body's timing.

Some circadian rhythm sleep disorders can go away on their own, but it depends on the type you're dealing with. Jet lag usually clears up within a few days as your body adjusts to a new time zone. But most chronic circadian rhythm sleep disorders don't resolve without changes to your sleep schedule, light exposure, or daily habits. The sooner you start addressing it, the more manageable the shift becomes.

Not quite, though circadian rhythm sleep disorder and insomnia can feel similar. Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep, no matter the time of day. A circadian rhythm sleep disorder is sleep happening at the wrong time. Someone with delayed sleep phase disorder, for example, might sleep just fine from 3am to 11am, instead of a more typical schedule.

The time it takes to reset your circadian rhythm depends on how far your body clock has shifted. Jet lag typically settles within a few days, but a significantly delayed or advanced sleep schedule can take several weeks of consistent habit changes to correct. Light therapy and melatonin can speed the process along, but there's no quick fix.

Melatonin can help with circadian rhythm sleep disorders, but the timing matters. For delayed sleep phase disorder, a low dose taken several hours before your target bedtime can help shift your clock gradually. For jet lag, taking it closer to your target bedtime tends to work better. A doctor or sleep specialist can help you figure out the right dose and timing for your situation.

If your sleep schedule has been getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life—and adjusting your habits hasn’t helped—it's worth reaching out to a doctor or sleep specialist. They can assess whether you have a circadian rhythm sleep disorder and recommend a treatment plan.

💙 Learn more about the 7 most common sleep disorders.

In many cases, you can fix your circadian rhythm naturally. Focus on getting bright light in the morning and keeping consistent sleep and wake times. For milder patterns, these changes alone can make a noticeable difference, though more serious cases may need extra support.

#9405. Early Puberty More Common in Girls with ADHD

Neurodivergent girls are more likely to experience early puberty and may be especially vulnerable to its effects. Here, understand why.

Puberty is not a single event, but a years-long process that is both universal and highly individual. It shapes brain and emotional development, identity, and lifelong physical and mental health. If it begins before a child is developmentally ready, it can increase the risk for physical and mental health problems.

Research suggests that girls with ADHD are more likely to enter puberty early and to experience the transition more intensely, placing them at heightened risk for anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and other challenges. Parental guidance, emotional regulation skills, and professional support can buffer these risks by bolstering self-confidence in girls as they navigate the pubertal transition.

Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children.1 In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.

Early relative puberty — development that begins earlier than average but remains within the typical age range — is different from precocious puberty. In girls, precocious puberty refers to physical and hormonal changes before age 8, including breast and pubic hair development, rapid growth, and menstruation. It requires medical evaluation and treatment. Left unmanaged, it can contribute to shorter adult height, psychosocial distress, and other complications. Two forms exist:

Rising hormone levels affect the physiological and neural systems involved in emotional processing and regulation.

Girls who menstruate may also experience pronounced changes in ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle.

Girls who mature early may feel distressed when their physical development outpaces their cognitive, emotional, and social development.
