#9289. 2 Personality Traits Are Linked to Lower Inflammation

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.

Among the qualities that make up conscientiousness, being hardworking and organised stood out.

For extraversion, which includes both sociability and energy, the clearest result was for people who described themselves as active.

These patterns matter because inflammation that stays elevated over time is linked to both physical and psychological health.

Lower levels of long-term inflammation are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, stroke and premature death.

They have also been associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

The researchers pooled data from six studies involving more than 19,000 adults in the United States, England and Japan.

Participants rated how well words such as ‘organised’, ‘hardworking’ and ‘active’ described them.

The researchers then looked at how those answers related to two markers of inflammation in blood samples, C-reactive protein and interleukin-6.

Earlier research had already linked higher conscientiousness with lower levels of both inflammatory markers (Luchetti et al., 2014).

In this study, people who described themselves as organised or hardworking tended to have lower levels of both markers.

Being hardworking showed the strongest association within conscientiousness, even stronger than the association for the overall trait score.

People who scored higher on extraversion tended to have lower C-reactive protein, and much of that association came from how active they said they were.

In fact, being active was more strongly associated with lower C-reactive protein than any other characteristic the researchers examined.

Being talkative showed a small association in the opposite direction, while being lively was associated with lower levels of both inflammatory markers.

In several of the studies, the association with being active held up even after the researchers took other aspects of extraversion into account.

Being active and hardworking may both reflect how much energy people have for everyday tasks.

In earlier research, people who scored higher on the activity aspect of extraversion or the achievement-striving aspect of conscientiousness tended to have better aerobic capacity during a brisk walking test (Terracciano et al., 2013).

Regular physical activity could help explain part of the association with inflammation.

The relationship could run in the other direction, too, if people with higher inflammation feel less energetic and come to see themselves as less active or lively.

The study was published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology (Stephan et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9288. Umberto Eco’s Antilibrary: Why Unread Books Are More Valuable to Our Lives than Read Ones

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:

Partial to Bitcoin? You can beam some bit-love my way: 197usDS6AsL9wDKxtGM6xaWjmR5ejgqem7

Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

“It is our knowledge — the things we are sure of — that makes the world go wrong and keeps us from seeing and learning,” Lincoln Steffens wrote in his beautiful 1925 essay. Piercingly true as this may be, we’ve known at least since Plato’s famous Allegory of the Cave that “most people are not just comfortable in their ignorance, but hostile to anyone who points it out.”. Although science is driven by “thoroughly conscious ignorance” and the spiritual path paved with admonitions against the illusion of thorough understanding, we cling to our knowledge — our incomplete, imperfect, infinitesimal-in-absolute-terms knowledge — like we cling to life itself.

And yet the contour of what we know is a mere silhouette cast by the infinite light of the unknown against the screen of the knowable. The great E.F. Schumacher captured this strange dynamic in the concept of adaequatio — the notion that “the understanding of the knower must be adequate to the thing to be known.” But how do we face our inadequacy with grace and negotiate wisely this eternal tension between the known, the unknown, the knowable, and the unknowable?

That’s what Lebanese-American scholar, statistician, and essayist Nassim Nicholas Taleb explores in a section of his modern classic The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable (public library) — an illuminating inquiry into the unknowable and unpredictable outlier-events that precipitate profound change, and our tendency to manufacture facile post-factum explanations for them based on our limited knowledge.

Taleb uses legendary Italian writer Umberto Eco’s uncommon relationship with books and reading as a parable of the most fruitful relationship with knowledge:

The writer Umberto Eco belongs to that small class of scholars who are encyclopedic, insightful, and nondull. He is the owner of a large personal library (containing thirty thousand books), and separates visitors into two categories: those who react with “Wow! Signore professore dottore Eco, what a library you have! How many of these books have you read?” and the others — a very small minority — who get the point that a private library is not an ego-boosting appendage but a research tool. Read books are far less valuable than unread ones. The library should contain as much of what you do not know as your financial means, mortgage rates, and the currently tight real-estate market allows you to put there. You will accumulate more knowledge and more books as you grow older, and the growing number of unread books on the shelves will look at you menacingly. Indeed, the more you know, the larger the rows of unread books. Let us call this collection of unread books an antilibrary.

Eco himself has since touched on humanity’s curious relationship with the known and the unknown in his encyclopedia of imaginary lands, the very existence of which is another symptom of our compulsive tendency to fill in the gaps of our understanding with concrete objects of “knowledge,” even if we have to invent them by the force of our imagination. Taleb adds:

We tend to treat our knowledge as personal property to be protected and defended. It is an ornament that allows us to rise in the pecking order. So this tendency to offend Eco’s library sensibility by focusing on the known is a human bias that extends to our mental operations. People don’t walk around with anti-résumés telling you what they have not studied or experienced (it’s the job of their competitors to do that), but it would be nice if they did. Just as we need to stand library logic on its head, we will work on standing knowledge itself on its head.

Noting that his Black Swan theory centers on “our misunderstanding of the likelihood of surprises” because we underestimate the value of what we don’t know and take what we do know “a little too seriously,” Taleb envisions the perfect dancer in the tango with knowledge:

Let us call this an antischolar — someone who focuses on the unread books, and makes an attempt not to treat his knowledge as a treasure, or even a possession, or even a self-esteem enhancement device — a skeptical empiricist.

Complement The Black Swan, which is fascinating it its totality, with astrophysicist Marcelo Gleiser on how to live with mystery in a culture obsessed with certitude, philosopher Hannah Arendt on how unanswerable questions give shape to the human experience, and novelist Marilynne Robinson on the beauty of the unknown.

#9286. Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene

Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability.

Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a new path toward Alzheimer's treatments.

The discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene.

Fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it.

That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation?

A new study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process.

"This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," says Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

"We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection."

How an Alzheimer's Risk Gene Weakens the Blood-Brain Barrier

The blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste.

When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's.

To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity.

Their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice.

Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels.

In mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky.

Scientists Discover How Fibronectin Causes Brain Damage

One experiment provided especially important evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels.

The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly.

Increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally.

These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it.

"The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved."

The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage.

They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase.

These abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier.

When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage.

"Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling."

Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection

Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4.

Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid showed that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes.

Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an important role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels.

Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4.

"The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation.

A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire New Alzheimer's Treatments

The potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant.

Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal new opportunities for prevention and treatment.

The latest findings suggest several possible approaches.

One strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier.

Researchers are already investigating these possibilities through laboratory experiments.

However, translating the discovery into a treatment will require considerable care. Fibronectin performs essential functions throughout the body, including supporting tissue structure and helping damaged tissues heal. Any future therapy would therefore need to target its harmful accumulation or effects without disrupting these beneficial activities.

By identifying the molecular mechanisms involved, scientists now have a more precise framework for designing such treatments. The findings may also help researchers determine when interventions would be most effective and how to measure whether they are successfully protecting the brain.

"By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working," says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. "Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's to an early disease process that may be possible to modify."

Although these potential therapies remain experimental, the discovery offers a promising new direction in Alzheimer's research. Rather than focusing only on the damage that develops as the disease progresses, scientists may eventually be able to reproduce a natural genetic defense that helps protect vulnerable brains before significant damage occurs.

#9285. The Generosity of Selfishness: C.S. Lewis on How to Be Interesting

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. Our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in contemplating the nature of creativity. “You open your safe and find ashes.”

Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

C.S. Lewis (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir Surprised by Joy (public library).

With an eye to the ideal structure of the creative life, he writes:

It is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration.

This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”:

Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise.

Shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there.

Couple with John Steinbeck on the art of receiving, then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longing.

#9284. Objects reinstalled at Museo Nacional de Colombia following removal by right-wing government

Several items were removed from this display on 15 October Photo: Angie Matiz

Bogotá’s Museo Nacional de Colombia has reinstalled the 63 objects previously taken down from its permanent galleries over claims of “political indoctrination”. The move followed a court order that reversed the national government's removal of the items on 15 October.

On the evening of 28 October, César Enrique Osorio Ortiz—a judge at Bogotá’s 24th Family Court—ordered Colombia’s cultural ministry and the museum to return the works to their original locations within 48 hours. The ministry complied with the order on Friday (30 October).

The decision came in response to a constitutional-rights case filed by cultural groups and political opponents who had accused the government of the country's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella of censorship. The judge also ordered both institutions not to remove works based on their content or the views they express.

Among the removed pieces were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo, a pen made from a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 peace agreement between the state and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.

Empty spaces where items had been removed from the museum walls Courtesy Colombia Diversa

The removals came amid calls by De la Espriella for a “cultural war” and a “direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture”, an offensive that affected the country’s main museum.

The government’s decision sparked a series of protests during which hundreds of people gathered outside the museum, as well as a joint statement by six museums expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of their professional autonomy. The signatories included the Modern art museums of Bogotá, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellín and Tolima, as well as the Museo Rayo.

Marielsa Castro Vizcarra, the chief curator of the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (which signed the joint statement), tells The Art Newspaper that the cultural sector responded quickly, from street protests to the statement and the involvement of the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art. Castro described the incident as “a precedent we need to take into account” and “an authoritarian way of spreading fear”.

According to the judge's ruling, the artefacts had been removed “without a documented curatorial justification” in a decision that “disregarded the constitutional protection of cultural expressions”. The court did not rule out future changes to the exhibitions, provided they are properly justified and not based on the authorities’ objections to the works’ content.

“No government owns our history!” wrote Gabriel Becerra, a left-wing lawmaker behind the constitutional-rights case, in a post on X welcoming the court’s decision.

#9283. Are You Making This Common Mistake With Grief?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In recent years, the language of therapy has moved beyond the clinic and into everyday conversation, giving us new ways to name our inner lives and, at times, new ways to misread them. Nowhere is this more evident than in how we respond to grief.

In grief, we learn quickly which words help and which ones wound. “At least they lived a long life.” “They wouldn’t want you to be sad.” Most of us recognize these as unhelpful sentiments.

Not all harmful responses to grief sound like clichés, though. Sometimes they arrive dressed in compassion, wrapped in the language of awareness. A friend might say, “This seems to be activating your abandonment wound,” “Maybe this pain is really about your father,” or “Maybe this is more about your unhappiness in your marriage.” The words may be well-intentioned, even psychologically accurate, yet the effect can be deeply unsettling. Instead of feeling seen, we feel studied; instead of comforted, diagnosed.

This dynamic can feel like a kind of gaslighting because the tools and language of healing are used to explain away your emotions instead of tending to them. Unlike gaslighting in the usual sense, it isn’t malicious. It’s the experience of being told what your pain really means instead of having that pain simply met. It is a byproduct of a therapy-literate culture that often privileges interpretation over presence.

For the past several years, I’ve taught death and dying at the university level and led grief retreats. Again and again, I’ve watched grief ease, not when someone explained it, but when someone stayed with it. In what follows, I’ll look at how analysis can crowd out presence, and offer ways to stay with grief, someone else’s or your own, without rushing to interpret it.

When we’re grieving, people want to help, but few things wound more than having sorrow dissected while it’s still unfolding. Well-meaning insight can become a form of distance. A loved one may believe they’re offering understanding when they say, “This loss must be reminding you of when you lost your job,” or “You seem to struggle with change, don’t you?,” yet the grieving heart hears something different: that the pain belongs to something older and is therefore less legitimate.

Both can be true. A new loss often awakens older ones, but truth without warmth is just analysis. The body doesn’t sort its ache into past and present; it simply calls for accompaniment. In one well-known study, holding the hand of a trusted person calmed the brain’s response to threat, no words required. Seeing where a present loss touches earlier wounds can be deeply healing, eventually. But categorizing pain does not lessen the need to feel it.

We can also engage in this kind of gaslighting internally. Once we have absorbed enough psychological language, we can turn the same clinical lens on ourselves. We catch the echo of a past wound and then scold our grief for being disproportionate. “I’m overreacting,” we tell ourselves. “This is just my old stuff.” “Why can’t I just be happy?” Yet grief does not care how insightfully we label it. It still needs space to breathe. Awareness can be a form of care, but only when it does not rush ahead of the feeling itself. If it becomes a strategy to bypass feeling, our own or another’s, it defeats itself.

Many guests arrive at our retreats saying some version of “I should be over this by now.” Over the days that follow, that urgency to be finished often quiets, not through argument, but because the grief is finally given room. On the last day, they complete a ritual deep in the forest, at a fountain carved with the outline of a family. Around it, they leave rocks painted with the names of the people they’ve lost. The oldest rocks have since faded almost past recognition, the paint softening into a weathered imprint.

I’ve come to see this not as loss, but as integration: the sharp color of a fresh wound, still seeking an explanation, settling into something that no longer needs to announce itself. No one stood over the rocks interpreting them. They simply bore witness. Grief often becomes more endurable in exactly this way: when it is allowed to change shape in the space of time, care, and presence.

These suggestions come from years of sitting with grieving people, and from my own experience of loss. They are less techniques than reminders of what the moment is asking for.

Resist the urge to explain. The interpretive reflex—reaching for meaning, context, or psychological framing—is often a response to our own helplessness in the face of grief’s rawness. Notice when you’re doing it, pause, and return to the simpler question: Can I be here with this person, without needing it to mean something right now?

Let the silence be full rather than empty. Many people fill silence because it feels like abandonment. A silence in which you remain present, your body in the room, your attention undivided, can be the most companioning thing you offer. “I’m here,” said once and then honored, is worth more than 10 minutes of careful insight.

Follow their lead on meaning. If the grieving person begins to find meaning themselves, to name connections, to speak about what this loss is touching in their past, that is theirs to do. Your role is to witness it, not to initiate it. There is a world of difference between meaning that emerges from the griever and meaning that is handed to them. When you catch yourself doing it, try asking a different question: What does this need? Usually the answer is simpler than any interpretation: company, time, permission to be exactly this intense.

If you feel the pull to theorize about someone else’s grief, a few questions can help you track it in time: Am I trying to ease their pain, or my own discomfort with it? Did they ask for insight, or am I offering it uninvited? Have I acknowledged the loss itself, fully, before reaching for what it might mean?

When you’re unsure what to say, three phrases rarely go wrong: “Tell me about them.” “What do you miss most today?” “I’m here.” Each one keeps the person grieving at the center.

Grief has a way of making us distrust our own experience. We begin measuring whether we’re grieving correctly, whether we’ve stayed sad too long or not long enough, or whether the intensity means something beyond the loss itself.

Catch the self-diagnosis. This one is not easy, because the narrating voice sounds so reasonable: “This is really about my mother,” “I’m being too sensitive,” “I’m being disproportionate.” It rarely announces itself as unkind.

Notice when you’re applying the same analytical approach to yourself that you’d resist from someone else. Then let the intensity of the feeling stand without demanding it justify itself first.

Ask your grief what it needs, not what it means. Meaning can come later, if it comes at all. In the acute moment, the more honest question is practical: You might need rest, someone to call, permission to cancel a plan. Let the meaning-making wait.

Choose your witnesses. Some people simply cannot stay in the uncertainty that grief creates. Their discomfort shows up as advice, reassurance, or psychological evaluation. It doesn’t make them uncaring. It simply means they may not be the people to rely on in the rawest moments of loss. Notice who can sit in the room without needing to fix or explain, and lean on them more.

Insight has a place in grief. In time, many people do come to see how one loss is woven through the others, and that understanding can bring relief. But it tends to arrive on its own schedule, after the pain has been felt and met. Until then, what we can offer, to someone else or to ourselves, is company. The rocks at the fountain didn’t fade because anyone explained them. They faded because they were left where they were, held by time and by the people who stood beside them. Even when a wound is old, the tenderness it requires is always immediate.

Naomi Sanderovsky, Ph.D., is the founder of Luma Via retreats and trainings, and the creator of Living Grief Theory and Felt Sense Dynamics. She has taught world religions, global philosophy, and more recently death and dying at the university level for more than 20 years.

#9282. Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

Growing older is often associated with memory loss and declining mental abilities. However, scientists are questioning whether these changes tell the whole story. Rather than simply becoming less capable, the brain may be adapting to a new stage of life in which accumulated knowledge, wisdom, and understanding become more important than remembering every detail.

Researchers at the University of Arizona have proposed a different way of understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on findings from molecular biology and brain imaging, they suggest that the changes occurring in older brains may reflect a natural stage of human development rather than deterioration alone. Their work, published in Perspectives on Psychological Science, offers a new perspective on why thinking and memory change with age.

The researchers call their proposed explanation the adaptive aging hypothesis. It suggests that the brain gradually adjusts its priorities to make better use of a lifetime of accumulated experience. This could help explain why older adults often have valuable strengths in teaching, mentoring, storytelling, and passing knowledge to younger generations.

"If we look at normative aging as a story of just decline, we are really missing the boat," said study coauthor Fabian-Xosé Fernandez, an associate professor of cognition and neural systems at the University of Arizona. "The older brain is optimized for different things than the younger brain, predominantly the sharing of stored expertise and social relationships."

How the Brain Shifts From Memory to Meaning

Two brain regions play important roles in how people remember and interpret their experiences. The hippocampus helps preserve specific information about events, including their details and circumstances. The frontal cortex, meanwhile, is more involved in extracting broader meaning, recognizing patterns, and understanding the central message of an experience, sometimes called its "gist."

According to the researchers, the balance between these systems changes during healthy aging. As people grow older, the brain tends to place less emphasis on activity in the hippocampus and rely more on the frontal cortex. This shift may allow the brain to focus more on interpreting information through existing knowledge rather than recording every new experience in precise detail.

"The fact that you see this across people and animal models suggests there is an evolutionary driving force," Fernandez said. "One could argue you are developing your entire life, and development occurs in lockstep with the needs of your brain. When you're younger, the hippocampus turns on because you don't have a knowledge base or know how the world works. A kid absorbs information like a sponge because they are building an archive of information. In early life, the balance is tilted toward recollecting declarative memories with precision, detail, and context."

Young brains need to gather enormous amounts of new information because they are still building a foundation for understanding the world. By later adulthood, however, people have already developed extensive stores of memories, concepts, and experiences. Connecting new information to what they already know may become more useful than retaining every individual detail.

The researchers suggest that this changing balance reflects a shift in how the brain processes experience. Instead of concentrating primarily on collecting detailed memories, it increasingly emphasizes understanding relationships, identifying underlying meaning, and applying previously acquired knowledge.

Why Evolution May Favor Wisdom in Older Adults

Evidence of similar changes in animal models raises the possibility that this transition has an evolutionary explanation. Fernandez suggests that the aging brain may be adapting to help individuals preserve and share the knowledge they have acquired throughout their lives.

From this perspective, the ability to draw on decades of experience could be especially valuable for making judgments, guiding others, and transferring important information between generations. Older adults may therefore play a distinct role in supporting younger people through mentorship, teaching, and storytelling.

"Given those goals, it makes sense that you aren't interested in nitty-gritty details," Fernandez said. "You are interested in safeguarding the vast knowledge you already have. Evolution may be saying that if you make it long enough, there's a need to transmit this information, so we put into motion biological changes that enforce and protect your semantic and autobiographical memories."

Under this hypothesis, changes in memory and thinking are not necessarily signs that the brain is functioning less effectively. They may instead reflect a different set of priorities, with greater emphasis on preserving meaningful knowledge and using it to understand new situations.

Why Healthy Brain Aging Is Different From Alzheimer's

The adaptive aging hypothesis could also provide scientists with another way to examine the differences between normal cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease.

Although both involve changes in memory, Fernandez emphasizes that Alzheimer's should not be understood as ordinary aging taken to an extreme. The biological processes involved are fundamentally different.

"When I was in grad school, people thought about Alzheimer's as a more intense version of cognitive aging, but that is just not the case," Fernandez said. "They are completely different."

During typical aging, the brain's gradual shift away from relying heavily on the hippocampus and toward greater involvement of the frontal cortex generally unfolds between the fifth and seventh decades of life. In Alzheimer's disease, however, abnormal processes involving proteins such as amyloid and tau may interfere with this transition.

One important distinction involves activity in the hippocampus. While healthy aging is generally associated with reduced emphasis on this region, Alzheimer's can involve unusually high levels of hippocampal activity. Rather than supporting the normal progression of cognitive development, disease-related changes may disrupt the brain networks responsible for memory and understanding.

"In normative aging, hippocampal activation is deemphasized, which is probably what should be happening in a 70-year-old. But in many cases of Alzheimer's, it turns out the hippocampus is hyperactive," he said. "This beautiful developmental transition is completely disrupted in Alzheimer's disease by pathological processes that mess with episodic memory and interfere with circuits that allow you to think about your own life, lexicon, and vocabulary."

These disruptions can affect the ability to recall personal experiences and access stored knowledge, including words and their meanings. Understanding how these changes differ from the adaptations associated with healthy aging may help researchers develop a clearer picture of normal brain development and neurodegenerative disease.

Embracing the Hidden Strengths of the Aging Brain

The researchers argue that society may need to reconsider what successful brain aging looks like. Encouraging older adults to process information exactly as younger people do may not always be the most productive approach.

Fernandez suggests that placing excessive emphasis on remembering precise details could work against the brain's changing priorities. "For many individuals, the weight of how you process information should probably not be so hippocampal-centric by the sixth or seventh decade."

Instead of judging older adults primarily by abilities that tend to weaken with age, the researchers encourage greater recognition of the capabilities that may become especially valuable later in life.

Creating more opportunities for social interaction could be one way to support these strengths. Relationships between older and younger generations may be particularly beneficial because they provide opportunities to exchange experiences, share expertise, and preserve knowledge that might otherwise be lost.

"People see older individuals and look at them as not being on par with younger individuals across a lot of metrics," Fernandez says. "The way I look at it is that you've got someone with a brain that has been active for several decades and has seen a lot. There is tremendous value there, and we don't do a good job of unlocking it."

The central message of the adaptive aging hypothesis is that growing older may involve more than a gradual reduction in cognitive abilities. Although some mental skills become less reliable with age, the brain may also be adapting to make better use of the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime. Recognizing those strengths could change how society understands aging and the contributions older adults can make.

Several years ago, rummaging through the archives of the Academy of American Poets, I came upon a box labeled “Ballots 1950” — the record of the secret vote by the chancellors the year the Academy’s prestigious fellowship was awarded to E.E. Cummings, catapulting him into renown. The voting process is a black box — no one outside the Academy ever finds out who else is in the running and by how much the winner wins.

Leafing through the ballots, one other name appeared over and over, so much so that I was impelled to count.

Marianne Moore had lost by one vote, never knowing how close she had come. It would be many more years until, at 77, she was finally awarded the fellowship.

Long before that, before she won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award (sharing a table with Rachel Carson at the ceremony), Moore had set down her views on writing in a series of essays later collected in the out-of-print gem Predilections (public library). Pulsating through them is a reckoning with the impossible task of the writer — to weave tapestries of truth and meaning from the tenuous thread of words on the ramshackle loom of language.

In an essay titled “Feeling and Precision,” Moore writes:

Feeling at its deepest — as we all have reason to know — tends to be inarticulable. If it does manage to be articulate, it is likely to seem overcondensed, so that the author is resisted as being enigmatic or disobliging or arrogant.

How we name what we feel is not so much a matter of our writing style as of our style of being, because in order to articulate something we must first apprehend it and we apprehend every smallest thing with the whole person — with the frame of reference that is our entire life, the sum of our experience and memory. When “one of New York’s more painstaking magazines” asked Moore to distill her poetic style into a formula, she fought back the “dictatorial” reflex to quip:

You don’t devise a rhythm, the rhythm is the person, and the sentence but a radiograph of the personality.

And yet a personality can write with more or less persuasion — that is, write more or less well — depending on what the person brings to the writing. In another essay from the collection, Moore identifies the three psychological elements necessary for persuasive writing: “humility, concentration, and gusto.” A generation after Mark Twain assured his friend Helen Keller when she was accused of plagiarism that “substantially all ideas are second-hand, consciously and unconsciously drawn from a million outside sources,” she writes:

Humility… is armor, for it realizes that it is impossible to be original, in the sense of doing something that has never been thought of before. Originality is in any case a by-product of sincerity; that is to say, of feeling that is honest and accordingly rejects anything that might cloud the impression.

By “concentration” Moore means a kind of discipline — annealing the essence of the sentiment by cutting away all superfluous explanations, elaborations, and distractions of stylistic posturing, being maximally truthfully in the most minimal way possible. Observing that there is always a “helpless sincerity which precipitates a poem” and that a good poem is always “a concentrate,” she writes:

Concentration — indispensable to persuasion — may feel to itself crystal clear, yet be through its very compression the opposite… I myself would rather be told too little than too much.

Long before we had the language of extrinsic and intrinsic motivation, of finite and infinite games, Moore uses a lovely word, now dusty, for that peculiar private zeal propelling all creative work with its twin dynamos of discipline and deliverance: “gusto.” Echoing Rachel Carson’s abiding advice on writing — “If you write what you yourself sincerely think and feel and are interested in,” she had counseled a young writer, “the chances are very high that you will interest other people as well.” — Moore offers:

Gusto thrives on freedom, and freedom in art, as in life, is the result of a discipline imposed by ourselves. Moreover, any writer overwhelmingly honest about pleasing himself is almost sure to please others.

She maps the fundamental relationship between the three:

Humility is an indispensable teacher, enabling concentration to heighten gusto.

When creating in integrity with these three values, it ceases to matter how the work is received because the process of locating and articulating the truth as you feel it, the world as you see it, is its own reward. In what may be the best advice I have encountered on how to orient to your own work, Moore writes:

There are always objecters, but we must not be sensitive about not being liked or not being printed… The thing is to see the vision and not deny it; or care and admit that we do.

Complement with Walt Whitman on how to keep criticism from sinking your soul and Mary Oliver’s advice on writing, then savor the moving story of how Marianne Moore saved a rare tree with a poem.

#9280. Russia’s security service detains teen over alleged terror plot targeting Moscow museum

The Tsaritsyno palace in Moscow Photo courtesy the office of the mayor of Moscow, via Wikimedia Commons

Russia’s FSB security service has detained a teenager on charges of threatening Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve via TikTok after an unusual warning from US officials of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” on 31 October. The alert was posted on the website of the US embassy in Moscow and social media. Der Spiegel reported that German citizens in Russia had received a similar warning.

On 1 November, the FSB distributed a video, published on sites such as Tass, the official state news agency, showing an unidentified young man being detained, footage of a knife, camouflage and neo-Nazi content on his phone, and his confession to posting “propaganda of Nazism” on his TikTok page. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee posted the same footage to its YouTube channel.

The US issued a similar alert several days before an attack that killed at least 149 people in March 2024 during a concert at Crocus City Hall in Moscow. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack; before it occurred, Russian President Vladimir Putin denounced the warnings as “outright blackmail”.

In a change reflecting US President Donald Trump’s cooperation with Russia, the FSB in a statement on 1 November, posted on the agency’s website, credited “US law enforcement agencies” for warning of an impending attack at Tsaritsyno: “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”

The FSB statement added that “in the interest of public safety, planned cultural events at the museum-reserve have been cancelled, and security measures in the surrounding area have been stepped up”. The museum is typically closed on Mondays, while the surrounding park, known for its rolling hills, fountains and wooded paths, is open daily. Russian media reported that the park reopened on Sunday.

The FSB’s statement claims the detained minor had posted images on TikTok “showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, cap, eyewear and headset—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon” as well as “photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, accompanied by the caption: ‘I found a place’”.

The complex, which was originally intended as a summer residence for Catherine the Great in the 18th century, is consistently ranked as one of Moscow’s most visited tourist sites. Tsaritsyno’s website states that over 7 million people visit the museum and park in southern Moscow annually. The Grand Palace, its centrepiece, is known for its neo-Gothic design by the architect Matvey Kazakov, which remained unfinished after Catherine’s death. Many other buildings on the grounds were designed by Kazakov’s teacher, Vasily Bazhenov, Catherine’s court architect, who was initially commissioned to design the palace before falling out with the Empress.

Some preservationists denounced the glitzy completion of the palace, inaugurated in 2007 with Putin present. It was carried out under Moscow’s mayor at the time, Yury Luzhkov, who was known for monumental construction projects. Although some attempts have been made to show contemporary art at Tsaritsyno, its exhibitions are primarily focused on the tsars and historic Russian folk crafts.

As the Moscow institution is temporarily closed and its director, Roman Romanov, is dismissed, fears grow that Russia’s past is being glossed over

Landmark site was the burial place of Prince Grigory Potemkin, whose bones were removed by Russian occupying forces last year

The Pushkin design satellite will have both historic and contemporary design galleries

Zelfira Tregulova, who has headed the State Tretyakov Gallery since 2015, will be replaced by Elena Pronicheva, who has links to Vladimir Putin

#9279. Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit

Millions of Americans take fish oil supplements in hopes of protecting their memory and keeping their brains healthy as they age. These products have become a major business, with Americans spending more than $1 billion each year on supplements containing omega-3 fatty acids. These essential nutrients help build and maintain the connections between brain cells that support memory, learning, and other cognitive functions.

But a new study suggests that getting more omega-3s into the brain through supplements may not provide the protection many people expect.

Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC found that even when high doses of omega-3s successfully reached the brain, they did not produce measurable improvements in memory, thinking abilities, or protection against brain shrinkage.

The findings, published in eBioMedicine, come from a two-year clinical trial involving older adults considered to be at increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. Despite taking omega-3 supplements daily, participants showed no significant cognitive advantage over those who received a placebo.

"We all wish there was a silver bullet for preventing Alzheimer's, but our findings showed that fish oil supplements do not appear to protect brain health," said Hussein Naji Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health and lead investigator of the study. "While omega-3s play an important role in forming brain cell connections needed for cognition, our results do not support fish oil supplements as a preventive measure against Alzheimer's."

A Two-Year Study Tests Fish Oil's Brain Benefits

To investigate whether omega-3 supplements could protect the aging brain, researchers enrolled 365 adults between the ages of 55 and 80. All participants rarely ate fish, a major dietary source of omega-3 fatty acids, and were considered at elevated risk for Alzheimer's disease.

Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4, a gene variant associated with a substantially higher risk of developing Alzheimer's later in life. Although having this variant does not mean someone will necessarily develop the disease, it is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's.

Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a daily fish oil supplement or a placebo, an inactive treatment used for comparison. The supplements provided 2,000 mg of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 fatty acid that is especially important for the brain.

DHA is a major component of brain cell membranes, helping maintain the structure and function of neurons. It also supports communication between nerve cells, making it an important nutrient for normal brain activity.

The study was double-blind, meaning neither participants nor researchers knew who was receiving the active supplement during the trial. This approach helps reduce bias and makes it easier to determine whether any observed benefits are actually caused by the treatment.

Omega-3 Levels Rose, but Memory Did Not Improve

Before evaluating whether the supplements improved brain health, researchers needed to answer a fundamental question: Were the omega-3 fatty acids actually reaching the brain?

To find out, they measured DHA concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord. Examining this fluid can provide information about substances entering and circulating within the central nervous system.

After six months, DHA levels in the cerebrospinal fluid had increased by an average of 17% among participants taking the supplements. This provided evidence that the omega-3 fatty acids were reaching their intended destination.

However, getting DHA into the central nervous system was only part of the goal. The more important question was whether those higher levels would translate into better brain health.

Researchers assessed participants' memory and other cognitive abilities at the beginning of the trial and again after two years. Despite the increase in DHA, those taking fish oil performed no better on the cognitive tests than participants receiving the placebo.

Brain imaging revealed similarly disappointing results.

The supplements did not prevent shrinkage of the hippocampus, a region deep within the brain that plays a central role in forming and organizing memories. The hippocampus is particularly vulnerable to changes associated with aging and Alzheimer's disease, making its size an important indicator researchers use when studying brain health.

Taken together, the results suggest that simply increasing DHA availability in the brain is not enough to produce measurable cognitive benefits in this group of older adults.

Why Fish Oil Supplements May Work Differently Than Food

The unexpected findings have raised a new question for researchers: If omega-3s can reach the brain, why don't higher levels necessarily improve its function?

Yassine and his colleagues are now investigating how the brain absorbs, processes, and uses these nutrients. Their earlier research suggests that omega-3s may be more beneficial when consumed as part of a broader dietary pattern rather than taken in isolation as a supplement.

One possibility involves the Mediterranean-style diet, which emphasizes foods such as fish, vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and olive oil. This eating pattern naturally supplies omega-3 fatty acids alongside other nutrients and has been associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

The researchers suspect that the combination of nutrients in a balanced diet, along with an individual's overall health, may influence how effectively omega-3s support the brain.

"We're focused on better understanding how the brain processes omega-3s and whether factors, such as poor health, dietary pattern, genetic risk and age, may change the brain's ability to effectively absorb and use omega-3s," said Yassine. "We are working to develop medications that may help the brain better utilize these nutrients to preserve cognitive function."

Understanding these differences could eventually help scientists identify why certain people might respond better to omega-3s than others and whether new treatments could improve the brain's ability to benefit from these essential fats.

Importantly, the findings do not mean omega-3 fatty acids are unnecessary or that eating fish offers no health benefits. Instead, they indicate that taking high-dose DHA supplements alone did not provide measurable protection against cognitive decline or hippocampal shrinkage in the population studied.

Healthy Habits Remain Key to Alzheimer's Prevention

Although the trial focused specifically on fish oil supplements, the researchers emphasize that protecting brain health requires a much broader approach.

Rather than relying on a single supplement, they recommend maintaining healthy habits throughout life, including regular physical activity, sufficient high-quality sleep, and a nutritious, balanced diet.

These behaviors support overall health and may help reduce factors associated with cognitive decline. Physical exercise, for example, promotes cardiovascular health and blood flow, while sleep plays an important role in memory formation and normal brain maintenance.

"Staying healthy throughout life remains the most powerful tool we have for reducing Alzheimer's risk, including regular exercise, quality sleep and a balanced diet," said Yassine. "Living a healthy lifestyle is the brain's equivalent of getting regular car maintenance and high-quality oil changes. The brain is more likely to lose greater function if health issues in other parts of the body go unaddressed, in the same way that car engines stop working if regular maintenance is skipped."

While these lifestyle factors were not directly tested in the trial, the researchers believe they offer a more promising foundation for long-term brain health than depending on fish oil supplements alone.

The results also highlight an important distinction: A nutrient can be essential for healthy brain function without providing additional protection when consumed in large doses as a supplement. Understanding why that happens may open new avenues for research into Alzheimer's prevention and the nutritional needs of the aging brain.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, grant numbers RF1AG076124, R01AG055770, R01AG067063, R01AG054434, R21AG056518, P30AG066530 and R01AG054434 and the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation, grant number GC-201711-2014197.

#9278. The Clearest Sign Of The Winter Blues

Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9277. Can Well-Being Give You Two More Years of Life?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Decades of scientific inquiry have found that the quality and length of a person’s life goes up when they experience less depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions. More recent studies of psychological well-being—also referred to as happiness, flourishing, thriving, or the good life (among other terms)—have been reporting positive links to health and longevity.

For many, this combination of findings raises a question: “Does human mortality depend on the presence of human happiness and flourishing, or merely on the absence of mental health symptoms or bad feelings?”

That’s what Max Genecov and David S. Yeager explored in a recent meta-analysis, which combined findings from 99 different studies that measured mental health symptoms and conditions, well-being scores, and lifespan. Importantly, all the studies that they drew from used a longitudinal method, which means they took measurements repeatedly over time to explore whether momentary scores or score changes over time (e.g., well-being in early adulthood, or improvement in well-being) correspond with later scores or changes in another factor (such as the age or cause of death).

Well-being is generally understood as a combination of regularly feeling positive emotions, being satisfied with your life, and having a sense of meaning and purpose in life; ill-being reflects frequent and persistent negative emotions, chronic dissatisfaction, and purposelessness.

To get at this question of whether mental ill-being and well-being over time had overlapping, combined, or independent effects on all-cause mortality, Genecov and Yeager used a statistical approach that allowed them to correct for multiple factors under consideration. Their method was able to mathematically enumerate the impact of well-being on mortality while subtracting any coexisting impact of mental health challenges on mortality.

Why? Because if well-being and ill-being exist on a continuum, where reducing mental health conditions is ultimately the same as increasing well-being, then subtracting out the effects of ill-being would erase any concurrent benefit of higher well-being to mortality. But, if improving well-being and reducing ill-being independently affect mortality, where deteriorating mental health conditions and rising well-being contribute separately to how long a person lives, then their model would show distinct advantages of higher well-being to longevity above and beyond reducing symptoms of ill-being.

The result? In this study, people with higher-than-average well-being did live longer—and, indeed, this effect occurs above and beyond the lifespan advantages of lower-than-average ill-being. As the researchers sum up their results:

People one standard deviation above the average on well-being die at a 14% slower rate than those with average well-being. . . . As a practical reference using death probabilities from a 2020 United States Social Security Administration actuarial life table, a standard deviation increase on well-being corresponds to just under two years of more life for both men and women.

They saw older adults and patient populations with greater well-being live longer, and they also found people living longer who rated high in optimism, life satisfaction, positive emotion, a sense of social support, and purpose in life. This result isn’t new in the research, but by looking at the effects of ill-being, they were able to clarify its relationship to well-being and longevity. In fact, Genecov and Yeager found that the lifespan boost documented in their study (which controlled for the possible benefits of alleviating ill-being) was comparable to other studies of well-being and longevity that didn’t control for ill-being. This suggests that prior studies have also been capturing the unique and separate benefit of well-being to health and longevity.

While easy to grasp why, for example, less chronic stress would lead to better cardiovascular health and so a longer life, it’s not as clear from a scientific perspective why or how better overall well-being could help someone live longer. Right now, we know that optimism, positive emotion, social support, and purpose are associated with a longer life—we’re just not sure why, exactly.

That said, there are many ways mental well-being could fuel a longer and better life. More optimistic people, for example, tend to make healthier choices around physical exercise and diet, and to not smoke cigarettes. Positive emotions are linked to investing more effort toward and pursuing goals in life. People who score higher on measures of well-being are more socially appealing, generous, and compassionate toward others, and enjoy higher-quality friendships. One of the most famous studies of longevity attributes survival most strongly to supportive social bonds.

While still an emerging science, those findings suggest that well-being and related factors evoke experiences and motivate behaviors that measurably strengthen physical health in life-lengthening ways. While eliminating ill-being may diminish risks, obstacles, and barriers to physical health, fostering well-being may optimize physical systems to enhance stability, efficiency, and strength—both ultimately contributing to longevity but in different, often intersecting, ways.

Want to do more to enhance your well-being? The Greater Good Science Center has an entire website dedicated to supporting people who’d like to increase well-being called Greater Good in Action. You can explore and tinker with over 150 well-being–promoting activities, exercises, and practices drawn from published research, join a four-week Pathway to Happiness program, or try the seven-day Big JOY project.

Emiliana R. Simon-Thomas, Ph.D., is the science director of the Greater Good Science Center, where she directs the GGSC's research fellowship program and serves as a co-instructor of its Science of Happiness and Science of Happiness at Work online courses.

“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.

Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

In her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies, Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech.) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:

Our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.

Comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

#9274. Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles

Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves. However, common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) are an unusual exception. These small monkeys have brains that are almost entirely smooth, with very little folding. Scientists at the German Primate Center (DPZ), the Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen, have now identified several cellular processes that help explain this difference.

Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans. These differences involve the cells' structure, the speed at which they divide, and the timing of their development. Together, these changes reduce the number of neurons produced, contributing to the smaller size and smoother surface of the marmoset brain. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide new insights into primate brain evolution and could eventually improve our understanding of human brain development disorders.

Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded

Brain size and the extent of surface folding are important features that distinguish different primate species. The human brain, for example, has a highly folded surface resembling the ridges and grooves of a walnut. This arrangement greatly expands the brain's surface area, creating room for billions of neurons that support complex thinking and other advanced mental abilities.

Scientists believe that the common ancestor of modern primates already possessed a moderately sized brain with at least some folding. Yet not all primates living today retain these characteristics.

Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), small monkeys native to South America that are becoming increasingly important in biomedical research, have brains with almost no visible folds. Researchers at the German Primate Center set out to determine why their brains develop so differently from those of humans and other primates.

"We wanted to understand which changes at the cellular level cause the marmoset brain to grow less and form fewer folds," explains Lidiia Tynianskaia, one of the study's two first authors and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution at the DPZ. "At the beginning of development, the common marmoset brain exhibits the typical structure and composition of a large, folded primate brain. As development progresses, processes must therefore occur that effectively slow down the production of nerve cells."

Scientists Discover What Slows Brain Growth

To investigate these developmental differences, the team compared brain organoids grown from human and common marmoset cells. Their attention centered on neural progenitor cells, the cells responsible for generating neurons during brain development.

These progenitor cells play a major role in determining the eventual size and shape of the brain. The more neurons they produce, the greater the potential for the cerebral cortex to expand and develop folds.

The researchers found that the marmoset's smaller, smoother cerebral cortex is not the result of a single developmental change. Instead, several differences involving distinct types of progenitor cells work together to limit neuron production and brain folding.

"Our investigations have shown that certain progenitor cells in the common marmoset divide significantly more slowly than in humans," explains César Mateo Bastidas Betancourt, also a first author of the study and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group. "Other progenitor cells have a simpler structure than their human counterparts, with fewer processes, and are therefore less proliferative. Both of these factors ultimately result in fewer nerve cells, which contributes to a smaller size and less folding of the cerebral cortex in marmosets."

The scientists also identified important differences in when certain progenitor cell characteristics and behaviors emerge during development. Compared with humans, marmosets have a shorter overall period during which these cells can multiply rapidly.

Together, the slower rate of cell division, simpler cell structures, and shorter window for rapid growth help explain why the marmoset brain produces fewer neurons and develops far fewer folds.

Miniature Brains Reveal Important Developmental Clues

Much of the research relied on brain organoids, small, three-dimensional structures grown from cells that reproduce important features of early brain development. These miniature models allowed scientists to investigate developmental changes across multiple samples and compare the timing of key processes.

"The study combines the advantages of in vivo and in vitro methods," says Michael Heide, head of the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution. "Organoids are well-suited for obtaining statistically robust results because such sample sizes are not feasible in primates. We subsequently repeated some key experiments in fetal brain tissue to confirm the results from the organoids."

One particularly important finding involved the relationship between development in organoids and development in actual marmoset brains. The researchers determined that a marmoset brain organoid grown for 50 days closely matches the developmental stage of a natural marmoset brain at day 90.

Establishing this relationship was essential because brain organoids and actual brains do not necessarily develop at the same rate. By identifying corresponding developmental stages, the scientists could make meaningful comparisons and interpret their experimental findings more reliably.

What Smooth Monkey Brains Reveal About Human Brain Evolution

The findings help explain how relatively small differences in the behavior and developmental timing of brain-building cells can contribute to major differences in brain size and folding among primates.

They also offer a potential explanation for how the wide variety of primate brain shapes and sizes emerged over evolutionary time, including why some species developed relatively smooth brains while others possess much larger, heavily folded ones.

Beyond their evolutionary significance, these discoveries provide a foundation for investigating how the human brain develops and what happens when those processes are disrupted. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that control neuron production and brain growth could ultimately help researchers study developmental disorders affecting the human brain.

Materials provided by Deutsches Primatenzentrum (DPZ)/German Primate Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Three years after he became the second-youngest laureate of the Nobel Prize, awarded him for literature that “with clear-sighted earnestness illuminates the problems of the human conscience,” Albert Camus (November 7, 1913–January 4, 1960) died in a car crash with an unused train ticket to the same destination in his pocket. The writings he left behind — about the key to strength of character, about creativity as resistance, about the antidotes to the absurdity of life, about happiness as our moral obligation — endure as a living testament to Mary Shelley’s conviction that “it is by words that the world’s great fight, now in these civilized times, is carried on.”

Camus addressed his views on writing most directly in a 1943 essay about the novel, included in his altogether indispensable Lyrical and Critical Essays (public library).

One must be two persons when one writes… The great problem is to translate what one feels into what one wants others to feel. We call a writer bad when he expresses himself in reference to an inner context the reader cannot know. The mediocre writer is thus led to say anything he pleases.

In a sentiment James Baldwin would echo in his advice on writing, insisting that “beyond talent lie all the usual words: discipline, love, luck, but most of all, endurance,” Camus observes that all creative endeavor demands of us “a certain constancy of soul, and a human and literary knowledge of sacrifice.” He writes:

To someone who asked Newton how he had managed to construct his theory, he could reply: “By thinking about it all the time.” There is no greatness without a little stubbornness.

Nearly a century after Tchaikovsky asserted that “a self-respecting artist must not fold his hands on the pretext that he is not in the mood,” Camus adds:

Great novels… prove the effectiveness of human creation. They convince one that the work of art is a human thing, never human enough, and that its creator can do without dictates from above. Works of art are not born in flashes of inspiration but in a daily fidelity.

Complement with more excellent advice on writing from Mary Oliver, Rachel Carson, Maya Angelou, George Saunders, John Steinbeck, and Ernest Hemingway, then revisit the beautiful letter of gratitude Camus sent to his childhood teacher shortly after receiving the Nobel Prize.
